content.prompt: Part 1 — A newspaper article and a mysterious connection
content.answer: The story opens with its narrator, a boy named Michael, reading a newspaper article headlined "Miracle Recovery," reporting that a fourteen-year-old schoolboy named Sebastian Shultz, whose condition had been critical after a car accident and a resulting coma, has unexpectedly recovered. Michael is startled because he realises this is the very same Sebastian Shultz he had "met," in a strange and indirect way, weeks earlier while playing a series of computer games. The article prompts Michael to look back and piece together exactly what had happened to connect him to a boy he had never met in person.
content.notes: Frame narrative: the newspaper article as the trigger for Michael's recollection.

content.prompt: Part 2 — The Computer Fair and the first strange message
content.answer: Michael recalls that, a month earlier, he and his technology-obsessed father, who could never resist buying the latest computer gadgets and gizmos, had spent an entire Saturday afternoon at a computer fair, where his father bought him a virtual reality visor and glove along with a handful of the latest interactive psycho-drive games. Playing the 3D game "Wildwest," Michael takes on the role of a sheriff and is drawn into a duel-and-chase sequence with a mysterious second sheriff who never answers when questioned about his identity; after gunfire and the game abruptly ending with a score of 21095, Michael's printer produces an unexpected printout showing the figure of the sheriff and a message: the player is stuck inside the game and needs help to be retrieved, signed "Sebastian Shultz," who suggests Michael try the game "Dragon Quest" next.
content.notes: Establishes the fantastical premise: a real boy's memory trapped inside game software.

content.prompt: Part 3 — Further games and growing understanding
content.answer: Following the instructions in each successive printed message, Michael plays through further games — including "Dragon Quest," in which his task is to rescue Princess Aurora from a wicked dragon and gather its treasure, and later "Jailbreak" — always encountering the same trapped companion, Sebastian, who urges him onward and hints at his predicament. Michael gradually works out, partly with his father's help understanding how computers store data, that Sebastian's actual memory had somehow become saved onto the game disks themselves at the moment of his real-world accident, when he had been playing one of these very games and struck his head, falling into a coma. The disks, stolen from the Shultz household after the accident, had eventually made their way, through unknown hands, to the computer fair where Michael's father purchased them.
content.notes: Explains the mechanism: Sebastian's memory recorded onto the disks during his accident.

content.prompt: Part 4 — The rescue in Warzone and the miracle recovery
content.answer: In the final game, "Warzone," Michael and Sebastian devise a plan together — using a helicopter to pull Sebastian to safety as a tank crashes into a jeep — and this time, at last, Michael successfully retrieves Sebastian from the trapped state within the game. At the very same moment in the real world, doctors are astonished to find that Sebastian, previously in a critical coma, suddenly and inexplicably begins to recover — the "miracle" reported in the newspaper article Michael reads at the story's opening. The story closes with Michael reflecting on how strange and yet undeniably real this virtual connection has proven to be, leaving him — and the reader — to wonder just how "virtually true" the boundary between the game world and reality really is.
content.notes: Climax and resolution: the in-game rescue coincides with Sebastian's real recovery.

content.prompt: The blurred boundary between virtual reality and the real world
content.answer: The story's central and title-defining idea is that the line between a virtual, simulated experience and genuine reality may be far less solid than it appears. Sebastian's memory, physically recorded onto game software during his accident, is not merely symbolic but has a real, tangible effect on his actual medical recovery once Michael manages to "rescue" him within the game world. Paul Stewart uses this science-fiction premise to invite readers to consider how deeply technology might one day intertwine with human consciousness and experience, well beyond simple entertainment.

content.prompt: Empathy, help, and connection across distance
content.answer: Despite never meeting in person and having no ordinary means of communication, Michael persists across several separate games, guided only by cryptic printed messages, to help a boy he does not know. His willingness to keep playing, puzzle through clues, and ultimately devise a rescue plan for Sebastian reflects a theme of compassion and cooperative problem-solving extended toward a stranger in genuine need, even when the situation defies rational explanation.

content.prompt: Curiosity and the wonder (and danger) of new technology
content.answer: Michael's father's enthusiasm for the latest computer gadgets sets the entire plot in motion, reflecting society's fascination with rapidly advancing technology. The story simultaneously celebrates this curiosity — it is precisely this fascination that allows Michael to help Sebastian — and hints at technology's unpredictable, even dangerous potential, since it was an accident involving deep immersion in a "psycho-drive" style game that caused Sebastian's coma in the first place. This dual perspective encourages readers to consider both the possibilities and the risks of ever more immersive computer technology.

content.prompt: Michael
content.answer: Michael is the story's young narrator, an enthusiastic player of computer games who becomes unexpectedly and inexplicably drawn into a real rescue mission through a series of virtual game worlds. Curious, persistent and ultimately compassionate, he does not give up on the mysterious companion who keeps appearing in his games, working with increasing understanding to figure out what is happening and how to help. His role in Sebastian's eventual, "miraculous" recovery gives him — and the reader — a lasting sense of wonder about how real virtual experiences can actually be.

content.prompt: Sebastian Shultz
content.answer: Sebastian Shultz is a fourteen-year-old schoolboy from South London whose real-world car accident, occurring while he was playing one of the very computer games later purchased by Michael's father, leaves him in a critical coma. Remarkably, his memory becomes saved within the game software itself at the moment of the accident, trapping a version of his consciousness inside successive games, from which he repeatedly and politely requests Michael's help through printed messages. His patient, hopeful persistence across multiple failed attempts, and his relief and gratitude once finally rescued, make him a sympathetic figure whose real-world recovery is directly tied to events inside the virtual games.

content.prompt: Michael's father
content.answer: Michael's father is depicted as thoroughly enthusiastic about computers and new technology, unable to resist buying the latest gadgets and gizmos whenever he encounters them, which is precisely how the crucial game disks first enter the household during their visit to the computer fair. Beyond providing the games that set the plot in motion, he also offers Michael some technical understanding of how computers store and retain data, which helps Michael begin to make sense of Sebastian's strange, persistent presence within the games.

content.prompt: Mr Shultz (Sebastian's father)
content.answer: Mr Shultz appears only briefly, in a press conference reported after Sebastian's accident, where he is asked by a reporter what the family intends to do next regarding the stolen computer games; he replies simply that they will buy new ones, showing little interest in tracing the missing disks. This small detail turns out to be significant, since it is precisely because the stolen disks are never recovered that they are free to circulate onward and eventually reach the computer fair where Michael's father buys them, unknowingly setting the story's central rescue in motion.

content.prompt: What does the story teach about persistence and helping others in difficulty?
content.answer: The story shows that persistence, even when a situation seems strange or difficult to understand, can make a genuine difference to someone in need. Evidence: Michael does not give up on Sebastian despite repeated failed attempts across different games, eventually working out, with his father's help, a successful plan in "Warzone" that finally rescues him. The lesson is that patient, sustained effort to help someone, even a stranger encountered under unusual circumstances, can lead to a meaningful, life-changing outcome.

content.prompt: What does the story suggest about approaching new technology with both curiosity and caution?
content.answer: The story presents technology as a source of both wonder and unpredictable risk. Evidence: Michael's father's enthusiastic collection of the latest gadgets ultimately enables Sebastian's rescue, yet it was Sebastian's own deep immersion in a similar game that led to the accident and coma in the first place. The lesson is to appreciate the possibilities technology offers while remaining mindful that it can also carry real, sometimes serious, consequences.

content.prompt: What newspaper article does Michael read at the beginning of the story, and about whom?
content.answer: He reads an article headlined "Miracle Recovery" about a schoolboy named Sebastian Shultz, who had unexpectedly recovered from a critical coma.

content.prompt: Where did Michael and his father get the computer and games that begin the story's events?
content.answer: They bought them during a Saturday afternoon spent at a computer fair, which Michael's technology-obsessed father was eager to visit.

content.prompt: What happened when Michael played the game "Wildwest"?
content.answer: He became a sheriff in a 3D duel-and-chase sequence with a mysterious second sheriff, and after the game ended he received a printout signed by Sebastian Shultz asking for help.

content.prompt: What was Sebastian's first request to Michael, as shown in the printout?
content.answer: He said he was stuck and asked Michael to help retrieve him, suggesting he try playing "Dragon Quest" next.

content.prompt: What was Michael's task in the game "Dragon Quest"?
content.answer: He had to rescue Princess Aurora from a wicked dragon and collect the creature's treasure along the way.

content.prompt: How, according to Michael's theory, had Sebastian's memory come to be stored in the game disks?
content.answer: Sebastian's memory had been saved onto the disks during his accident, while he was playing the same game and struck his head, falling into a coma.

content.answer: The disks had been stolen from the Shultz household after Sebastian's accident and eventually found their way to the computer fair, where Michael's father purchased them.

content.answer: His idea was to use a helicopter to rescue himself, hoping it could move faster to escape the danger in the game.

content.prompt: How was Sebastian finally rescued, and in which game did this happen?
content.answer: In the game "Warzone," Sebastian tumbled into a helicopter when a tank crashed into a jeep, and Michael pulled him to safety, finally freeing him.

content.answer: Sebastian, who had been in a critical coma, suddenly and inexplicably began his "miracle" recovery, as reported in the newspaper article.

content.answer: He said he had not bothered tracing the stolen games and that he intended to simply buy new ones.

content.answer: It raises the question of how far a virtual, simulated experience can have genuinely real consequences, blurring the line between the game world and reality.

content.prompt: How does the story end, after Michael's final rescue of Sebastian in "Warzone"?
content.answer: It ends with Michael checking his e-mail later and finding a message from Sebastian thanking him and telling him to keep the games — he had earned them.

content.prompt: Trace how Michael comes to understand what is happening to Sebastian across the course of the story.
content.answer:
Structured answer:

Introduction: Michael's understanding of Sebastian's strange predicament develops gradually, built up through a series of odd encounters within different computer games.

Evidence: He first receives a puzzling printed message signed by "Sebastian Shultz" after playing "Wildwest," asking for help and directing him to another game. Through subsequent games such as "Dragon Quest" and "Jailbreak," Michael keeps encountering the same trapped companion, and with his father's help understanding how computers store data, he theorises that Sebastian's memory had become saved onto the disks during his real accident.

Conclusion: This step-by-step piecing together of clues across multiple games mirrors a detective-style unfolding of the mystery, culminating in Michael's successful rescue of Sebastian in "Warzone."

content.prompt: Discuss the theme of the blurred boundary between virtual reality and the real world in "Virtually True."
content.answer:
Structured answer:

Introduction: The story's title itself signals its central theme — that events inside a virtual, simulated game world can have genuinely real, even life-altering consequences.

Evidence: Sebastian's consciousness becomes physically trapped within the game software following his real-world accident, and his fate within the games — being rescued or remaining stuck — directly mirrors his actual medical condition, culminating in his real recovery at the exact moment Michael frees him in "Warzone."

Conclusion: By making the virtual and the real worlds causally connected rather than separate, Paul Stewart invites readers to question how solid the boundary between simulated experience and genuine reality truly is, especially as technology grows more immersive.

content.prompt: Explain the role that Michael's father plays in the events of the story.
content.answer:
Structured answer:

Introduction: Although Michael's father never directly interacts with Sebastian, his enthusiasm for technology is the essential catalyst that sets the entire plot in motion.

Evidence: It is his eagerness to buy the latest computer gadgets at the fair that brings the crucial, stolen game disks into their household in the first place. He later also provides Michael with basic technical understanding of how computers retain data, which helps Michael begin to make sense of Sebastian's otherwise inexplicable presence within the games.

Conclusion: Michael's father thus functions as both the unintentional cause of Michael's involvement and an indirect source of the knowledge that ultimately allows Michael to help resolve Sebastian's crisis.

content.prompt: What message does the story convey about persistence and compassion, illustrated through Michael's actions?
content.answer:
Structured answer:

Introduction: Michael's repeated efforts across several different, unrelated games to help a stranger he has never physically met demonstrate the story's underlying message about persistence and compassion.

Evidence: Despite the strangeness of the situation and several unsuccessful attempts, Michael continues following Sebastian's clues from game to game, eventually devising, together with Sebastian, a successful helicopter rescue plan in "Warzone." His willingness to keep trying, without any guarantee of success or personal benefit, ultimately contributes directly to Sebastian's real recovery.

Conclusion: The story suggests that genuine compassion and sustained effort to help others, even under bizarre or seemingly impossible circumstances, can produce meaningful, real-world good.
